paragraphs.heading: Heat and work in the air
paragraphs.text: Atmospheric thermodynamics is the study of how heat is turned into work inside Earth's atmosphere, and how work is turned back into heat. We experience the results of those exchanges as weather and climate. The field takes the laws of classical thermodynamics and uses them to explain things like the behavior of moist air, how clouds form, convection, boundary layer meteorology, and instability in the vertical direction.

paragraphs.heading: Rising and sinking air
paragraphs.text: A central idea is buoyancy. Warmer air is less dense, so buoyant forces lift it, while denser air sinks. The field also follows water as it evaporates from liquid into vapor and condenses back again. Differences in pressure from place to place change these movements, and the Coriolis force changes the motion that results. Taken as a whole, the air never sits in equilibrium: it is a non-equilibrium system.

paragraphs.heading: The toolkit
paragraphs.text: The working tools include the conservation of energy, the ideal gas law and specific heat capacities. Scientists also assume isentropic processes, meaning ones in which entropy stays constant, and moist adiabatic processes, during which no energy moves in or out as heat. Most of the gases involved are treated as ideal gases. Water vapor can shift between gas, liquid and solid and back again, and it is seen as one of the most important trace parts of air.

paragraphs.heading: From equations to forecasts
paragraphs.text: Adiabatic and diabatic forces acting on parcels of air are written into the primitive equations of air motion, either worked out on a grid or estimated below the grid's scale. Those equations underpin numerical predictions of both weather and climate. The field also provides the basis for how weather models handle cloud microphysics and convection. Thermodynamic diagrams help forecasters judge how storms will develop, and today the subject is an integral part of forecasting.

paragraphs.heading: Steam engines to the sky
paragraphs.text: In the early 19th century, Sadi Carnot, Rudolf Clausius and Émile Clapeyron built mathematical models of fluids and vapors tied to the cycles of steam engines, including the Clausius–Clapeyron equation. Papers in the 1860s took up dry and moist adiabatic processes in the atmosphere. In 1884 Heinrich Hertz devised the first atmospheric thermodynamic diagram, called the emagram. Von Bezold published a long work on the thermodynamics of the atmosphere in 1888, and Alfred Wegener published a book on the subject in 1911. The name itself can be traced to a 1919 publication by Frank W. Very.

paragraphs.heading: The Hadley circulation as an engine
paragraphs.text: The Hadley circulation can be treated like a heat engine. In it, warm, moist air rises near the equator and colder air comes down in the subtropics, and this circulation, driven by heat, produces kinetic energy. Treated as an engine, its efficiency stayed fairly steady from 1979 to 2010, averaging 2.6%. Over the same years the power it generated grew by about 0.54 TW per year, a sign of more energy flowing in that fits the observed trend in tropical sea surface temperatures.

paragraphs.heading: Hurricanes as heat engines
paragraphs.text: A hurricane can be modelled as a heat engine running between the sea, at about 300K (27 °C), and the tropopause, at about 200K (−72 °C), turning heat energy into the energy of wind. Air moving just above the sea picks up heat and water vapor, then rises, expands and cools, which brings condensation and rain. Treated this way, the storm follows a Carnot heat engine cycle that predicts its maximum intensity. A cooler upper troposphere or warmer air near the surface would each raise the strongest winds hurricanes reach.
